title: Exercise-associated hyponatremia and hydration status in 161-km ultramarathoners
authors: Hoffman MD, Hew-Butler T, Stuempfle KJ
population: Finishers of 161-km ultramarathons in northern California (5 years of data combined and reanalyzed); body weight before/after, post-race [Na] in a subset
findings: 887 finishers with body-weight data and 669 with post-race [Na]; EAH incidence 15.1% overall (range 4.6-51.0% by year), with a significant positive relationship with ambient temperature.

Among runners with EAH, 23.8% were overhydrated (weight change >= 0), 40.6% euhydrated (0 to -3%) and 35.6% dehydrated (< -3%); in this environment EAH was more common with dehydration than overhydration.
Weak relationship between post-race [Na] and body-weight change (r = 0.17, P < 0.0001): lower [Na] more common with more weight loss.
Faster runners tended to lose more weight (r = 0.092, P = 0.006); top finishers ranged from ~1% weight gain to ~6% loss.
Authors conclude weight loss > 3% does not seem to harm performance, so excessive sodium supplementation and aggressive fluid ingestion beyond thirst are ill advised.
limitations: Observational reanalysis of pooled data from one region and event type; correlations are weak; body-weight change is confounded by food, glycogen water and gut contents; cannot establish causation. Contrasts with the overdrinking mechanism emphasised in the 2015 consensus, so the finding that EAH was more common with dehydration should not be generalised.
implications: Do not prescribe fixed fluid volumes: 'drink to thirst' with an upper bound; treat weight gain as a flag.
Do not use weight loss up to ~3% as a stop or penalty trigger; hydration targets should not aim for zero weight change.
Heat modifier: more sodium awareness and monitoring in hot races (highest EAH incidence), without encouraging overdrinking.

verification.notes: Crossref match; all numbers confirmed in the Europe PMC abstract. Design kept as prospective-cohort although the paper is a pooled reanalysis of earlier prospective data.
